# Japan has endured 'lost decades' in research—and the slide is accelerating.

- Global paper output ranking: 2nd → 5th in two decades (NISTEP 2024)
- Top 1% cited papers: 5th → 12th—now trailing Spain and Iran
- University of Tokyo: 19th → 27th in global rankings; three other top universities dropped out of top 100
- Nature Index 2024: Japan's adjusted share fell 9.0% year-over-year

![Japan's research position is declining on every major metric—quantity, quality, and institutional prestige.](placeholder.png)

<!--
Speaker notes: Let me begin with an uncomfortable truth. Japan's research establishment has endured what many academics now call 'the lost decades.' The numbers tell a stark story. According to NISTEP's latest data, Japan has fallen from second to fifth place globally in total paper output. More concerning is the quality decline: we've dropped from fifth to twelfth place in the world's top 1% most-cited papers—now trailing countries like Spain and Iran. The University of Tokyo has slipped from 19th to 27th in global rankings, and three of our other top universities have dropped out of the top 100 entirely. This is not a temporary setback. The Nature Index confirms that Japan's contribution to high-quality research continues to decline. The question we must ask ourselves is: why is this happening, and what can we do about it?
-->

# Young researchers are fleeing academia—and the talent pipeline is breaking.

- PhD enrollments down 25% over 20 years (MEXT data)
- Only 123 new PhDs per million population—less than half of UK (313) or Germany (315)
- Tenured positions for researchers under 40: 23.4% → 15.1% (2007-2016)
- 'Low-paid, insecure jobs drove talented young researchers out' —Robert Geller, UTokyo

![Japan produces fewer PhDs than peers, and those who do enter academia face a rapidly shrinking path to job security.](placeholder.png)

<!--
Speaker notes: Behind these statistics are people—talented young researchers who are making difficult choices about their futures. PhD enrollments have fallen 25% over two decades. Japan now produces only 123 new doctoral recipients per million people—less than half of what the UK or Germany achieve. Why? Because the career path has become untenable. The share of tenured positions for researchers under 40 has dropped from 23% to just 15%. As Professor Robert Geller of the University of Tokyo puts it: 'The creation of a career ladder of low-paid, insecure jobs drove talented young researchers out of academia.' Some who earn PhDs are looking abroad for careers. Others simply choose different paths entirely. We are not just losing rankings—we are losing the people who would write Japan's next chapter in scientific discovery.
-->

# Traditional hierarchies and institutional silos are strangling innovation.

- METI 2012: Japanese companies 'hesitant to collaborate' and 'isolating from international R&D' (pattern persists per continued ranking declines)
- Foreign faculty at Japanese universities: <5% vs. UK's ~30%
- Silos between disciplines, theory vs. empirical, lack of diversity identified as barriers
- Bank of Japan: 'Low levels of collaborative innovation with outside companies and institutions'

![Japanese researchers are boxed in by four structural barriers that prevent the collaboration driving global innovation.](placeholder.png)

Speaker notes: But funding alone doesn't explain everything. There is a structural problem. A 2012 METI report documented something troubling: Japanese companies were hesitant to collaborate with other entities and were therefore falling behind in open innovation. While this data is from over a decade ago, the continued decline in Japan's research rankings suggests these structural barriers persist. Japanese universities remain strikingly insular—fewer than 5% of full-time faculty are from abroad, compared to nearly 30% in the UK. Research from the Bank of Japan points to low levels of collaborative innovation with outside companies and institutions. We have built walls where we need bridges—between disciplines, between institutions, between Japan and the rest of the world. These conclusions raised concerns that Japan might be isolating itself from the international R&D collaborations driving global research productivity. The good news is that this is a problem we can solve.
-->

# Domestic funding has stagnated—researchers are competing for a shrinking pie.

- National university operating grants: $87B (2004) → $76B (2022)—13% decline
- 2004 corporatization law enforced 1% annual cuts to operational support
- Research time for faculty: 46.5% (2002) → 37.2% (2008), largely unchanged since
- Competitive grants cannot compensate for cuts to baseline funding

![A 13% funding cut has forced researchers to spend less time on research and more on teaching and administration.](placeholder.png)

<!--
Speaker notes: The financial picture is equally concerning. When Japan's national universities were corporatized in 2004, the government steadily cut operating funds—from $87 billion in 2004 to $76 billion in 2022, according to the Japan Association of National Universities. That's a 13% decline in real resources. MEXT enforced 1% annual cuts to operational support. The consequence? Faculty research time dropped from 46.5% in 2002 to 37.2% by 2008 and has remained low ever since. More time goes to teaching and administration; less to discovery. While competitive grants have increased, they cannot make up for the erosion of baseline funding. Researchers are competing ever more fiercely for a shrinking pie. This is the 'what is'—a difficult present. But now let me share a vision of what could be.
-->
